summaries.example: Imagine the word “healthy.” A dog can be healthy. Food can also be called healthy, but the food is healthy because it helps the dog stay well. The word has connected uses, not exactly one use and not completely unrelated uses. Medieval thinkers used examples like this to explain analogy.
summaries.summary: Medieval thinkers developed theories of analogy to solve puzzles about language, logic, theology, and reality. They divided terms into three broad groups. A univocal term keeps the same sense. An equivocal term has unrelated senses. An analogical term has different but connected senses. For example, a dog is healthy in a direct way, while food is healthy because it helps produce health. Philosophers also asked how words such as “good” and “being” apply both to ordinary creatures and to God. They wanted language about God to be meaningful, while also recognizing that God is unlike created things. Aquinas explained such words through relatedness, causation, and participation: creatures have goodness or being in a dependent way, while God is goodness and being in an essential way. Scotus challenged important parts of this approach, especially by defending a unified concept of being. Later thinkers, including Cajetan, tried to explain how analogy could work in careful reasoning. The debate moved from words themselves to the concepts in people’s minds and how those concepts represent things.
key_ideas: Medieval philosophers studied analogy because words can have meanings that are the same, completely different, or related.
They were especially interested in words such as “being,” “good,” and “wise,” and in how people could speak about God.
Some analogies compare relationships, while others connect a main thing with things that depend on it.
Thomas Aquinas argued that words used of God and creatures are not exactly the same in meaning, but they are not meaningless either.
John Duns Scotus argued that the word “being” should have one unified concept so that philosophy and theology could reason about it.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic shows that using language well is not just about knowing dictionary definitions. We also need to notice how a word’s uses are connected, whether an argument keeps the same sense, and whether different ideas can be compared fairly. These questions still matter whenever people discuss big ideas such as reality, goodness, or God.

important_terms.definition: Using one word in different ways that are connected to one another.
Using a word with the same sense each time, such as “animal” for a person and an ox.
Using the same word for completely different things or ideas.
What a word points to or makes known, such as an idea or a thing.
The study of what exists and how different kinds of reality are related.

questions_to_think_about: Can one word have several related uses without becoming confusing?
How is calling food “healthy” different from calling a dog “healthy”?
What might happen if a word used in an argument changed meaning halfway through?
Why might people disagree about whether “being” has one meaning or several related meanings?

summaries.example: Consider the statement “This medicine is healthy” and the statement “The patient is healthy.” The patient has health directly; the medicine is healthy only because it produces or supports the patient’s health. This is analogy of attribution, in which one use is primary and another is dependent on it. By contrast, analogy of proportionality compares relations: a point can be called a principle of a line in a way related to how a spring is a principle of a river.
summaries.summary: Medieval theories of analogy were semantic and logical theories shaped by three larger problems. Logic needed to distinguish valid uses of a term from fallacies caused by equivocation. Theology needed to explain how finite human language could speak meaningfully about a transcendent and absolutely simple God. Metaphysics needed language for relations among substances and accidents, and between God and creatures. The basic vocabulary distinguished univocal terms, equivocal terms, and analogical terms. An analogical term has uses that differ but are related. Medieval authors described several forms. Proportionality compares two relations. Attribution orders uses around a primary case: an animal is healthy primarily, while food or urine is healthy through a causal or evidential relation to the animal. Imitation or participation concerns creatures’ dependent likeness to divine perfections. The classification was disputed, partly because “being” does not fit neatly into the ordinary categories. Aquinas held that divine names cannot be purely equivocal, since theology would then lose intelligibility, but cannot be strictly univocal, since God’s mode of being differs radically from that of creatures. He therefore appealed to analogy, while also distinguishing what a word signifies from its creaturely mode of signifying. Scholars disagree about how Aquinas’s various discussions fit together. Scotus rejected analogical semantics for “being” in his early logical work, then defended its univocity in later theology, arguing that a unified concept is required for metaphysics. Later Thomists such as Cajetan explored whether analogical terms involve one concept or several ordered concepts, and whether certain analogies can serve in demonstration. key_ideas: The theory arose at the meeting point of logic, theology, and metaphysics: philosophers had to explain equivocation, divine language, and relations among kinds of being.
Medieval authors distinguished analogy of proportionality, attribution, and imitation or participation, though they did not always classify them in the same way.
A major issue was whether analogy is a kind of deliberate equivocation or a genuine middle position between equivocation and univocity.
Aquinas used analogy to explain how names such as “good” and “wise” can be said of both God and creatures, while preserving their profound difference.
Scotus argued that “being” is univocal at the level of concept, because a unified concept is needed for metaphysics and theology.
Later Thomists, especially Cajetan, connected theories of analogy with the structure of concepts and with the possibility of valid syllogistic reasoning.
summaries.why_it_matters: The medieval debate clarifies a problem that appears throughout philosophy: how can one concept or word apply across important differences without collapsing those differences? It also shows that theories of meaning affect theories of reality and proof. Questions about whether “being” is analogical or univocal influence how philosophers understand metaphysics, theological language, concepts, and the possibility of demonstration.

important_terms.definition: A theory that a term has distinct but related applications rather than one identical sense or wholly unrelated senses.
A term used in exactly the same sense of different things.
A term whose applications have wholly different senses; medieval discussions also included deliberate, related forms of equivocation.
A use of analogy in which one analogate is primary and another is described through its relation to it, often as a cause, effect, or sign.
A use of analogy based on a similarity between two relations, such as the relation of a point to a line and a spring to a river.
A medieval account in which creatures reflect or share, in a dependent way, perfections associated with God.
The concept or act of understanding associated with a term; later medieval debates asked how many concepts an analogical term involves.
The claim that a term is linked to one concept that can apply to different realities without changing into unrelated meanings.

questions_to_think_about: If a word has related senses, what makes an argument using that word logically valid?
Does a comparison between two relations explain more than a comparison between two objects?
Can language about God be meaningful without claiming that God and creatures are the same kind of thing?
Is one unified concept of being necessary for philosophical reasoning, as Scotus argued?
When should a metaphor count as analogy, and when is it simply a new or improper use of a word?

summaries.example: Suppose someone says, “That meal is healthy” and “Maya is healthy.” Maya is healthy because her body is well. The meal is healthy in a different way because it helps her body stay well. The uses of “healthy” are connected, but they are not identical. Medieval philosophers called this kind of connection analogy of attribution. They also studied analogy of proportionality, such as comparing the way a spring begins a river with the way a point begins a line.
summaries.summary: Medieval theories of analogy grew from questions about how language works and how different kinds of reality are related. Medieval thinkers distinguished univocal terms, which have the same sense in each use, from equivocal terms, whose senses differ. Analogical terms were understood as having different but related senses. This idea helped address three problems. In logic, philosophers wanted to avoid arguments that secretly changed the meaning of a word. In theology, they asked how words such as “good,” “wise,” or “just” could be used of both God and human beings. In metaphysics, they needed to discuss things that exist in different ways, such as substances and their qualities, or God and creatures. The main types of analogy included proportionality, which compares relationships; attribution, which orders uses around a primary case; and imitation or participation, in which creatures resemble or share in a more fundamental perfection. Aquinas used analogy to argue that divine names are meaningful but not univocal: God’s goodness is not just another instance of human goodness, yet creaturely goodness is related to divine goodness through dependence and causation. His writings use more than one classification, and scholars disagree about whether this reflects development or differences in context. Duns Scotus took another route. He argued that “being” must be tied to one unified concept so that metaphysics and theology can reason about it, even though God and creatures remain radically different. Later Thomists, especially Cajetan, examined how concepts, abstraction, and syllogistic proof affect the theory. Thus the debate concerns not only vocabulary, but also the structure of thought and the kinds of reasoning philosophy can support.
key_ideas: Medieval philosophers used analogy to handle difficult cases in language, especially words applied to God and to created things.
They inherited a framework of univocal and equivocal terms from Aristotle and tried to place analogy within or between those categories.
Three important forms of analogy were proportionality, attribution, and participation or imitation.
Aquinas said that words such as “good” can apply to God and creatures in related ways, but not in exactly the same way.
Scotus criticized the idea that “being” must be analogical and defended a single concept of being for reasoning about substances, accidents, God, and creatures.
Later thinkers debated whether analogy depends on one ordered concept or on several connected concepts, and whether it can be used in sound demonstrations.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic teaches us to look closely at words that seem simple but carry several connected uses. It also explains why philosophers can disagree even when they use the same examples: they may have different theories about concepts, reality, or what makes an argument valid. These skills are useful for reading difficult texts and testing whether a comparison really works.

important_terms.definition: A word used in different but connected ways.
A word used with one shared sense, like “animal” when applied to a person and an ox.
A word used with different senses; the senses may be unrelated or deliberately connected, depending on the classification.
The way a word acts as a sign for an idea or something outside the mind.
An analogy in which one thing is primary and another is related to it as a cause, effect, sign, or tool.
An analogy that compares two relationships rather than simply comparing two objects.
The view that creatures have perfections by sharing in or reflecting a more primary perfection.
A concept or intellectual account connected with a word; medieval writers debated whether an analogical term has one or several.

questions_to_think_about: What makes two uses of a word related rather than completely different?
Why would a logician worry about a word changing sense in a syllogism?
Does saying that creatures participate in goodness explain how they are good, or only describe the relationship?
Why might Aquinas avoid both complete sameness and complete difference when speaking about God?
Which seems stronger for the word “being”: one broad concept or several related concepts?
